title: Queen against a pawn on the seventh
summary: With checks and pins, the queen puts the black king in front of its own pawn, and each time our king takes a step.
part.start.title: The staircase of checks
part.start.summary: Checks closer and closer to the pawn, until the black king stands in front of it.
part.cycle.title: The free move and the cycle
part.cycle.summary: With the black king in front of the pawn, our king takes a step. Then a pin and the staircase again.
part.quiet.title: The quiet move
part.quiet.summary: When the black king steps two files away, the queen moves next to the pawn without check.
part.pin.title: When promotion blocks the check
part.pin.summary: With the black king next to the promotion square, the pawn blocks the check by promoting. The answer is the pin.
part.letQueen.title: Letting the pawn promote
part.letQueen.summary: With our king close, the new queen can get mated. And if a knight appears, watch out for the fork.
part.block.title: When our king blocks a line
part.block.summary: A king standing on one of the queen's lines takes her checks away. Find the line that is left.
part.sixth.title: The pawn on the sixth, and the summary
part.sixth.summary: Alatortsev against Chekhover, 1937: one step earlier, even the bishop pawn loses. Then the practical challenge.
step.t_start: The black pawn is one square from becoming a queen, defended by its king, and our king is far away on a8. The queen alone cannot capture the pawn. Think: how can she win the time our king needs to arrive?
step.t_start.hint1: A pawn with its own king in front of it cannot move.
step.t_start.hint2: Look for checks from squares the black king cannot reach, each one a little closer to the pawn.
step.intro: It looks like a lost race, but it is not. Against a centre or knight pawn, the queen alone wins the time the king needs. The idea is to put the black king on e1, in front of its own pawn: there it blocks the pawn, and Black must spend a move to get out. The manuals have a name for the technique: the staircase. Each check leaves the black king fewer squares, until the only one left is the square in front of the pawn.
step.d_stairs: First watch the staircase on the other side of the pawn, with the black king on f2.
step.d_stairs.m1: 1.Qh4+. A check from far away, from a square the black king cannot reach. The queen already watches e1 along the diagonal.
step.d_stairs.m2: 1...Kf1. The king stays next to the pawn to defend it. The other squares lose faster.
step.d_stairs.m3: 2.Qf4+. One step closer, again from a square the king cannot reach.
step.d_stairs.m4: 2...Kg1. The king steps away to g1, but stays next to the promotion square.
step.d_stairs.m5: 3.Qe3+. The key square: from e3 the queen attacks the pawn and takes f2 from the king.
step.d_stairs.m6: 3...Kf1. The only move that still defends the pawn.
step.d_stairs.m7: 4.Qf3+. The last step. On g1 the king would drop the pawn, and the queen would capture it. Only e1 is left.
step.d_stairs.m8: 4...Ke1. In front of its own pawn. As long as the king stands there, the pawn cannot move.
step.stairs: Now you, on the other side, with the queen on g1 and the black king on d2. Drive it to e1 with checks, each one closer to the pawn, never touching the king.
step.stairs.hint: A check from a central square the black king cannot reach. Then another check a little closer.
step.stairs.done: A staircase of checks: 1.Qd4+, 2.Qe3+ and 3.Qd3+. In the end the black king had no choice. On c1 it would drop the pawn, and 4.Qxe2 would capture it. It went to e1, in front of the pawn. Starting with 1.Qf2, pinning the pawn, also worked.
step.t_front: After 3...Ke1, the black king stands in front of its own pawn, and our king is still on a8. Think: what do you do with this free move, and how do you hold the pawn when the black king steps aside?
step.t_front.hint2: When the black king goes beside the pawn, the two of them stand on the same rank.
step.idea: This is the position we are looking for. While the black king is on e1, the pawn cannot move. Black needs one move just to get the king out of the way, and that move is our gift: the white king takes a step towards the pawn. Then the queen forces the black king back to e1, and it all repeats. That is how the manuals show it, and how Danghiangmanh's training position shows it, where this line comes from.
step.d_tempo: Watch a whole cycle, as in the training position, after 3...Ke1.
step.d_tempo.m1: 4.Kb7! The free move. The pawn is blocked, and our king takes a step towards it.
step.d_tempo.m2: 4...Kf2. The king steps aside to free the pawn. Now e1 is open.
step.d_tempo.m3: 5.Qd2! A pin along the rank. If the pawn moves, the black king is in check. And with no check, the black king gets no chance to choose a square.
step.d_tempo.m4: 5...Kf1. The king defends e1 again and leaves the pin.
step.d_tempo.m5: 6.Qf4+. The staircase starts again, as in the first chapter.
step.d_tempo.m6: 6...Kg1. Going to e1 would be worse: the king would be back in front of the pawn at once.
step.d_tempo.m7: 7.Qe3+. From e3 the queen attacks the pawn and takes f2 from the king.
step.d_tempo.m8: 7...Kf1. The only move that defends the pawn.
step.d_tempo.m9: 8.Qf3+. The last step. On g1 the king would drop the pawn.
step.d_tempo.m10: 8...Ke1. Back in front of the pawn. The whole cycle earned one king step.
step.cycle2: After 8...Ke1, the black king is in front of the pawn again. Now you: do the cycle once more. First the free move and, when the black king steps aside, the pin, this time from the other side.
step.cycle2.hint: The king first, towards the pawn. Then the square on the second rank from which the queen pins the pawn to the black king.
step.cycle2.done: 9.Kc6 and 10.Qf2. The same pin, from the other side. Each cycle gives our king one more square, until it is close to the pawn and the queen can take it.
step.t_quiet: In the training-position line, after 11.Qd4+, the black king went to c1. Here it went to c2 instead, with 11...Kc2, two files away from the pawn. Think: what is the shortest way to put the black king back on e1?
step.t_quiet.hint1: Sometimes it is not a check.
step.t_quiet.hint2: A square next to the pawn that the black king cannot attack.
step.quietWhy: After 11.Qd4+ Kc2, the move is 12.Qe3! The queen stands next to the pawn and takes d2 and d3 from the king. The black king must go back to d1 to defend the pawn, and the check on d3 puts it on e1. The checks also win, but they leave the black king far away. The quiet move is the shortest way.
step.d_quiet: A line from the manuals, by Yasser Seirawan. After 1...Ke3, the black king went to the other side of the pawn.
step.d_quiet.m1: 2.Qh4! A quiet move. The queen watches e1 along the diagonal: if the pawn promotes, she captures. Without defending e1, the black king must come back.
step.d_quiet.m2: 2...Kd2. The king defends the promotion square again.
step.d_quiet.m3: 3.Qd4+. A check that pushes the king to the side.
step.d_quiet.m4: 3...Kc2. Now two files away from the pawn, as in the position you studied.
step.d_quiet.m5: 4.Qe3! Quiet again. The queen stands next to the pawn and takes d2 and d3 from the king.
step.d_quiet.m6: 4...Kd1. The only way to defend the pawn.
step.d_quiet.m7: 5.Qd3+. Along the d-file, the king only has e1.
step.d_quiet.m8: 5...Ke1. In front of the pawn. That is the free move for our king.
step.quiet: Now a knight pawn, on b2. The black king is on d2, two files away from the pawn. Find the quiet move.
step.quiet.hint: The queen next to the pawn, on a square the black king cannot attack, from where she takes c2 and c3 from it.
step.quiet.done: 1.Qb3! and, after 1...Kc1, 2.Qc3+ puts the king on b1, in front of the pawn. With a knight pawn, the technique is the same.
step.t_pin: So far the black king had squares on both sides of the pawn. Now it is in the corner, on a1, next to the promotion square, and our king has already reached e4. Think: how do you hold the pawn?
step.t_pin.hint1: Before giving check, look at what Black answers.
step.t_pin.hint2: A pawn tied to its own king cannot move.
step.pinWhy: The natural check, 1.Qg1+?, is met by 1...b1=Q, and the new queen even checks our king along the diagonal from b1 to e4. 1.Qh1+? and 1.Qf1+? are the same. With the black king next to the promotion square, the pawn blocks the check by promoting. The winning move is quiet: the queen goes to g7 and pins the pawn to the king along the long diagonal.
step.d_pin: Watch the pin and what comes after it.
step.d_pin.m1: 1.Qg7! The pin. If the pawn promotes, its own king is in check.
step.d_pin.m2: 1...Ka2. The king leaves the diagonal to free the pawn.
step.d_pin.m3: 2.Qf7+. A check that comes closer without touching. Going back to b1 or a1 would lose faster.
step.d_pin.m4: 2...Ka3. Out of the pin, the king threatens 3...b1=Q again: the queen has to watch b1.
step.d_pin.m5: 3.Qb7! The queen attacks the pawn along the b-file. If it promotes, she captures on b1. Now our king comes.
step.pinMove: Your turn. The same pawn, the queen on h5 and our king on d5. The checks are blocked by promotion. Pin the pawn and, when the black king leaves the pin, pin it again.
step.pinMove.hint: First the long diagonal. When the black king leaves it, the second rank.
step.pinMove.done: 1.Qe5 and 2.Qe2. A pin on the diagonal, then on the rank. 1.Qh8 also pinned, and so did 2.Qh2.
step.t_fork: Black has just promoted to a knight, with check: the knight on g1 attacks our king on f3. The king has five squares, and one of them throws the win away. Think: where does it go?
step.t_fork.hint1: See where the knight can jump with check.
step.t_fork.hint2: A jump that gives check and also attacks the queen is called a fork.
step.letqWhy: Before the answer, where does this knight come from? Go back one move, in a similar position: the pawn still on g2, the black king on h2, the queen on a4. So far the queen has held the pawn. With our king close, sometimes the right thing is to let the pawn promote, because the new queen comes too late: with 1.Kf3, our king takes g2 and g3 from the black king, and after 1...g1=Q the queen mates along the h-file.
step.d_letq: Watch what happens if the pawn becomes a queen.
step.d_letq.m1: 1.Kf3! The king lets the pawn promote. From f3 it takes g2 and g3 from the black king.
step.d_letq.m2: 1...g1=Q. The new queen comes too late.
step.d_letq.m3: 2.Qh4#. Mate along the h-file. The black king has no square, and the new queen cannot get in the way.
step.d_knight: That is why the best defence is something else: promoting to a knight, with check.
step.d_knight.m1: 1.Kf3! The same move: the king takes g2 and g3 from the black king, and a new queen would be mated.
step.d_knight.m2: 1...g1=N+. Promoting to a knight, with check. Without a new queen there is no mate, and the knight even wins a tempo.
step.d_knight.m3: 2.Kf2. The king gets out of check and attacks the knight. Here the queen is on a4, out of reach of every knight jump, and all five king squares would do.
step.d_knight.m4: 2...Nh3+. The knight escapes with check, but it cannot reach the queen.
step.d_knight.m5: 3.Ke3. Queen against knight wins: the queen will hunt the knight down or give mate.
step.fork: Now the position from the start of this chapter: the knight has just been born with check, and the queen is on c3. Where does the king go?
step.fork.hint: Before moving the king, see where the knight can jump with check. Does any of those squares also attack the queen?
step.fork.done: Right. 1.Kf4? allowed 1...Ne2+, a check on the king and an attack on the queen at the same time: the fork. 1.Ke3, 1.Ke4 and 1.Kg4 also won. With the king away from the fork, the queen hunts the knight.
step.t_block: A position from the manuals, by Müller and Lamprecht. Our king is on d5, close to the pawn, and still White does not win. Think: what is in the way?
step.t_block.hint1: Look at the queen's lines to the black king. Is any of them closed?
step.t_block.hint2: Along which file did the queen give the checks that drive the black king to e1?
step.block: Our king on d5 looks well placed, but it is in the way: it closes the queen's d-file. With the king on d5, d6 or d7, the queen loses the checks along the d-file and cannot drive the black king to e1: it is a draw. One step to the side and everything changes. When you bring the king closer, look at the lines the queen needs.
step.d_unblock: The same ending, with our king one square to the side, on e5.
step.d_unblock.m1: 1.Qd8+! The d-file is open, and the check comes along it.
step.d_unblock.m2: 1...Kc1. The black king runs to the side.
step.d_unblock.m3: 2.Qh4! A quiet move. The queen watches e1 along the diagonal, and the pawn cannot promote.
step.d_unblock.m4: 2...Kd1. The king defends the promotion square again.
step.d_unblock.m5: 3.Qd4+. Along the d-file again, which our king left open.
step.d_unblock.m6: 3...Kc1. The king steps away from the pawn, and the staircase goes on with 4.Qe3+.
step.blockMove: Now our king stands on a diagonal. Pawn on d2, black king on c1, our king on f4. Only one move wins.
step.blockMove.hint: The pin along the diagonal from c1 to h6 would be the natural idea. What is in the way?
step.blockMove.done: 1.Qc5+! Our king on f4 closes the diagonal: 1.Qg5? and 1.Qh6? pin nothing, and 1.Qh1+? is met by 1...d1=Q. Along the c-file, the check drives the black king away from the pawn, and 2.Qb4+ follows.
step.t_race: This is the ending of Vladimir Alatortsev against Vitaly Chekhover, at the 1937 Soviet championship in Tbilisi. White's a-pawn is one step from promoting, and Black's f-pawn is on the sixth rank, stopped by White's pawn on f2. Alatortsev decided to trade rooks with 69.Rc8. Think: after the trade, who wins the race, and where will the black pawn be when White's queen is born?
step.t_race.hint1: Count the moves until each pawn promotes.
step.t_race.hint2: The black pawn is blocked by White's pawn on f2. To free it, the black king has to spend moves.
step.raceWhy: After 69...Rxc8+ 70.Kxc8 Kxf2, the black king stands in front of its own pawn, and White promotes on the next move, with the black pawn still on the sixth rank. With a bishop pawn on the seventh and its king beside it, there are drawing defences, the subject of the next lesson. On the sixth there is still time: the queen has one move to get in the way.
step.d_race.m1: 69.Rc8! Alatortsev offers the trade. Without rooks, the a-pawn promotes first.
step.d_race.m2: 69...Rxc8+. Black has nothing better: every move loses.
step.d_race.m3: 70.Kxc8. Now it is a race, and the a-pawn is one step away.
step.d_race.m4: 70...Kxf2. The king captures the pawn that blocked its own and ends up in front of its own pawn. White promotes on the next move, with 71.a8=Q, and the game ended in a White win on move 75.
step.sixthMove: Now a made-up position with the same kind of pawn: a bishop pawn on c3, on the sixth rank, the black king on b2 and our king far away on h8. If Black gets to play 1...c2 with the king beside the pawn, Black gets the drawing chances of the next lesson. Only one move wins.
step.sixthMove.hint: The checks give the queen away or let the pawn advance. Look for a square from which the queen ties the pawn to its king.
step.sixthMove.done: 1.Qd4! pins the pawn along the long diagonal. After 1...Kc2, the black king stands in front of its own pawn, and our king can walk: 2.Kg7. Almost every check gave the queen away, and 1.Qe2+ only drew.
step.recap: To take with you. One: checks and pins, never touching the king, until the black king stands in front of the pawn; each time, our king takes a step. Two: when promotion blocks the check, look for the quiet move, the pin; when our own king closes one of the queen's lines, look for the line that is left. Three: with the king close, letting the pawn promote can be right, but first look at the knight jumps. And a pawn on the sixth, even a bishop pawn, still loses: stop it before the seventh.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge, from the starting position. Black defends well: sometimes the king runs away from the pawn instead of going in front of it. If the pawn is left alone, attack it. If not, do the cycle. Finish with mate.
history: When both sides race to queen and only one makes it, this is often what is left: a queen against a pawn one step from promotion. The queen beats almost every pawn, but not on its own and not any old way: it needs a technique, with checks and threats, that forces the enemy king to stand in front of its own pawn. Each time that happens, your king gains time to take a step closer. The technique is old and appears in every manual, from Reuben Fine in 1941 to Jesús de la Villa. In 1937, at the Soviet championship in Tbilisi, Vladimir Alatortsev beat Vitaly Chekhover this way: he traded rooks, queened first, and the queen, helped by the king, still stopped the bishop pawn. The exceptions, the edge pawn and the bishop pawn already on the seventh rank, have a lesson of their own.
ex.e05: The queen is attacked by the pawn. Where does she go?
ex.e05.hint: Running away is not enough: the queen has to keep holding the pawn.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Qh2: the pawn is pinned along the rank, and the best defence is the king going to f1. Then 2.Qf4+, and the king must choose between g1, in front of the pawn, and leaving it. Knight's pawn, same technique. 1.Qh4+ on the first move also won.
ex.e11: Alatortsev vs Chekhover, 1937: White has just queened on a8, and the black king went to e3. The bishop pawn is still on the sixth. Win.
ex.e11.hint: On the seventh, with its king beside it, the bishop pawn usually draws. Here it is still one square back: first put the queen on a central square where it attacks the pawn, then bring the king.
ex.e11.solution: 72.Qd5, as in the game: the queen attacks the pawn and watches the diagonal the black king would use. After 72...Kf2, our king walks: 73.Kd7 (or 73.Kc7). The game went on 73...Kg3 74.Ke6 f2 75.Qh1, and Black resigned. On the first move 72.Qa2, 72.Qc6, 72.Qb7 and the king moves 72.Kc7, 72.Kd7, 72.Kb8 and 72.Kd8 also win: with the pawn on the sixth, there is time.
ex.e12: Our king is close, on d4, and the pawn threatens to queen. There are four checks at hand. Does any of them win?
ex.e12.hint: After a check along the first rank, Black can block by queening. Look for a quiet move that ties the pawn to the black king.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qb5! pins the pawn on the b5-f1 diagonal: if it advances, its own king is in check. The checks do not work: 1.Qa1+, 1.Qb1+ and 1.Qc1+ are blocked by 1...e1=Q, and it is queen against queen; 1.Qxe2+ gives the queen away. After 1...Kf2, 2.Qf5+ or the pin along the rank, 2.Qb2, hold the pawn.
ex.e13: Our king is two steps from the black king, but it blocks the queen's d-file. Only one move wins. Which?
ex.e13.hint: You do not always need to stop the pawn. What happens if it queens with our king right next to the black king?
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kd3! If the pawn becomes a queen, 2.Qc2 is mate, because the king on d3 guards c2. The best defence is to promote to a knight with check, 1...e1=N+, and queen against knight wins: 2.Ke3 (or 2.Ke4, 2.Kd4). The checks do not help: 1.Qc1+ and 1.Qc2+ give the queen away, and our king closes the d-file.
ex.e14: A position by I. A. Horowitz, 1957. The bishop pawn is on the sixth, and our king on g7 is in the queen's way. Only one move wins.
ex.e14.hint: Against the bishop pawn, the queen wants to pin it along a diagonal to the black king. The long diagonal is closed by our own king. Do not start with a check.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Qh6!! The queen takes the h6-c1 diagonal. If 1...c2, 2.Qc1+ and the pawn falls. The best defence is 1...Kb1, and only 2.Qb6+ keeps the win, checking along the b-file. After 2...Kc1, the staircase goes on with 3.Qg1+ (or 3.Qe3+). The natural 1.Qh1+? allows 1...Kb2!, and there is no pin on h8, because our king is on g7: a draw.
ex.e16: Our king is on d4, the queen on h6, and the pawn on e2 threatens to queen. Only one move wins, and after it every move counts too. Find the way, one move at a time.
ex.e16.hint: The checks let the black king escape or give the queen away. Use pins, first on a diagonal, then on the rank. And remember: with our king close enough, letting the pawn queen can be the answer.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qh5! pins the pawn on the h5-d1 diagonal. After 1...Kd2, 2.Qh2! pins it again, now along the rank. After 2...Kd1, 3.Kd3! lets the pawn queen: 3...e1=Q would be mate with 4.Qc2. The best defence is 3...e1=N+, and 4.Kc3! keeps the knight off the good squares: it goes to g2, and 5.Qxg2 leaves king and queen against king. In the middle moves the checks also win, but slowly: here only the shortest path counts.
key.start: The black pawn is one step from queening, protected by its king. The queen still wins, with the white king coming from far away, in the opposite corner.
key.front: With checks, the queen has forced the black king to stand in front of its own pawn. At that moment the pawn cannot advance, and the white king gains time to take a step.
key.dang: The same technique, with the queen starting from the other side of the board: checks and threats until the black king ends up in front of the pawn.
key.block: Watch your own king: here it stands in the queen's way and blocks her line. The queen loses the checks she needed, and it is a draw.
practice: Now against the clock, or without it. The pawn is on the seventh and your king is far away. Staircase of checks, king in front of the pawn, one step at a time.
